frictionVectors.title: European energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control over hydrocarbons and uses pipeline and LNG exports to preserve strategic leverage with Europe. Price volatility and European diversification efforts limit that leverage over time.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure footprint
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain important in construction, transport, and industrial projects, but Algiers has largely preserved decision-making control and avoids excessive dependence on any single external partner.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector foreign dominance
frictionVectors.details: International firms remain central to offshore production, technology, and financing, leaving Angola exposed to declining output and external capital terms. Local-content policies have increased participation but have not displaced foreign operational control.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese debt and infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed infrastructure remains strategically important and debt-service pressures constrain Luanda's room for maneuver. Angola is diversifying toward Western and Gulf investors, but refinancing needs preserve substantial external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Northern security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity from the Sahel threatens northern communities, transport corridors, and prospective resource zones. Benin is strengthening border security and regional cooperation, but sustained insecurity could redirect public investment.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cotonou's growth depends heavily on regional transit, especially trade linked to Nigeria and Niger. Border disruptions and neighboring political tensions can quickly affect customs revenue, fuel access, and logistics sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond-market concentration
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has improved its negotiating position with major diamond partners and secured greater local value retention, but the economy remains highly exposed to global diamond demand and pricing.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Interest in copper, nickel, and other minerals is increasing, creating opportunities for diversification alongside pressure from foreign investors for favorable access. Strong institutions give Gaborone comparatively high control over licensing and infrastructure terms.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater state participation, local processing, and tighter oversight of gold production, reducing the influence of foreign operators. This increases sovereign capture but risks investment retrenchment and production losses.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Ouagadougou's expanding security relationship with Russia offers an alternative to Western partners but creates new dependence on external military support and opaque commercial arrangements. Insecurity continues to disrupt mining corridors and state access to resource zones.

highlights: Nickel ambitions meet financing and infrastructure constraints
Rwanda tensions ease but regional insecurity persists

frictionVectors.title: MINERAL DEVELOPMENT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Burundi seeks to develop major nickel reserves but remains dependent on foreign capital, technology, and transport infrastructure. Weak regulatory capacity limits domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: GREAT LAKES SECURITY SPILLOVER
frictionVectors.details: Instability in eastern DRC and lingering Burundi-Rwanda mistrust constrain border trade and security cooperation. External mediation remains important to prevent renewed escalation.

highlights: Atlantic geography strengthens strategic bargaining power
Tourism and imported energy remain structural vulnerabilities

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL INFRASTRUCTURE COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: European, Chinese, and US-linked actors compete for influence around ports, airports, maritime surveillance, and digital connectivity. Praia retains considerable leverage through diversified partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: TOURISM AND ENERGY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on foreign tourism, imported fuel, and external financing exposes the economy to shocks beyond government control. Renewable-energy expansion is improving resilience but remains incomplete.

highlights: Kribi corridor expands external leverage over trade
Oil, timber, and mining value chains remain weakly domesticated

frictionVectors.title: CHINESE INFRASTRUCTURE LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain central to major roads, energy projects, and port-linked infrastructure, creating financing and concessionary dependencies. Cameroon gains connectivity but captures limited downstream value.

frictionVectors.title: ANGLOPHONE CONFLICT AND RESOURCE ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest disrupts transport, agriculture, and investment while strengthening informal extraction networks. Oil, timber, and transport corridors remain vulnerable to armed-group pressure.

highlights: Mining governance remains fragmented and opaque

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY-MINING NEXUS
frictionVectors.details: Russian security personnel and aligned commercial actors retain influence around regime protection and mineral access. The arrangement expands Bangui's short-term security options while reducing transparency and sovereign bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: CORRIDOR AND BORDER INSECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Poor roads and insecurity along routes to Cameroon and neighboring states raise the cost of exporting diamonds, gold, and agricultural goods. Conflict spillovers from Sudan and the Democratic Republic of the Congo add pressure.

highlights: Oil revenues underpin a highly centralized state
Sudan war reshapes border security and external partnerships

frictionVectors.title: OIL DEPENDENCE AND FOREIGN OPERATORS
frictionVectors.details: Chad's fiscal and political system remains heavily dependent on oil production managed with substantial foreign technical and commercial involvement. Volatile output and opaque revenue allocation constrain broader sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: SUDAN BORDER CRISIS
frictionVectors.details: The Sudan conflict has generated large refugee flows, cross-border armed activity, and pressure on eastern Chad's limited infrastructure. International security and humanitarian support remain essential to state capacity in the region.

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte and maritime jurisdiction
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, sustaining a core sovereignty dispute and limiting Comoros' control over surrounding maritime resources. Migration management keeps the issue politically active.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: French, Gulf, and multilateral financing remains essential for ports, energy, and public infrastructure, narrowing Moroni's room to set independent development priorities.

frictionVectors.title: M23, Rwanda, and eastern corridors
frictionVectors.details: Conflict around North and South Kivu continues to weaken Kinshasa's territorial control and disrupt mining, trade routes, and border infrastructure. Regional mediation has not removed the risk of renewed offensives.

frictionVectors.title: Cobalt and copper bargaining power
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-led processing and mining interests remain deeply embedded while Western actors seek supply-chain access and strategic partnerships. Weak oversight limits the state's ability to convert mineral wealth into broad-based sovereignty and revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign oil operators and volatile prices continue to shape fiscal space, leaving Brazzaville vulnerable to external commercial and creditor pressure. Limited diversification constrains autonomous resource policy.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-linked infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction involvement in roads, ports, and public works provides needed infrastructure but can reduce negotiating flexibility when revenues weaken. French and other Western energy interests remain significant.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa sovereignty and trade rules
frictionVectors.details: European sustainability and traceability requirements could raise compliance costs for producers while challenging Abidjan's control over value addition. Processing investment is improving domestic capture but remains heavily foreign-backed.

frictionVectors.title: Northern security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence and instability in the Sahel continue to pressure northern borders, transport corridors, and security budgets. Côte d'Ivoire is strengthening regional partnerships while protecting its ports and growth model.

frictionVectors.title: Base competition and sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: American, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities generate revenue and diplomatic leverage but make Djibouti's security posture dependent on external powers. Competition around the Red Sea increases both bargaining power and strategic risk.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti's ports and logistics corridors are central to Ethiopian trade yet remain tied to foreign operators, creditors, and security interests. Debt and refinancing pressures can limit the government's control over infrastructure policy.

highlights: Suez and LNG remain strategic anchors

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile Water Security
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to oppose unilateral Ethiopian control over Nile flows, while negotiations remain vulnerable to renewed diplomatic escalation. Water scarcity makes the dispute a core sovereignty issue.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and External Financing
frictionVectors.details: IMF, Gulf, and other external financing support macroeconomic stability but increase outside leverage over state assets, currency policy, and infrastructure priorities.

highlights: Oil rents are entering structural decline

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining production and limited economic diversification leave the state exposed to foreign energy companies, commodity prices, and external technical capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Infrastructure Competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed construction and maritime projects offer strategic value but risk deepening dependence without transparent commercial returns or stronger domestic control.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline draws interest from Gulf states, Türkiye, and other external actors seeking maritime access. Any port or security arrangement could materially alter Asmara's autonomy and regional bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Regional War Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Tensions involving Ethiopia, Sudan, and the Red Sea security environment create pressure on Eritrea's borders and military posture. Limited transparency increases the risk of miscalculation.

highlights: Economic lifelines run through South Africa
Sugar and water remain strategic assets

frictionVectors.title: South African Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Trade corridors, customs arrangements, electricity links, and labor flows leave Eswatini highly exposed to South African economic and political conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Land Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Investment in agribusiness, manufacturing, and infrastructure can expand state capacity but may limit local control over land, water, and value chains.

highlights: Port access is a strategic priority

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Access Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia's search for dependable maritime access remains contentious with Somalia and other regional actors. External security partnerships could improve access while creating new sovereignty constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Internal Conflict and Infrastructure Security
frictionVectors.details: Conflict risks in Amhara, Oromia, and other areas threaten transport corridors, industrial projects, and state control over resource-producing regions. Political fragmentation also increases openings for foreign influence.

highlights: Junta-led transition seeks a larger state role in oil and mining
Libreville balances France, China, and Gulf investors

frictionVectors.title: Mining and oil renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are pressing for greater domestic value capture from manganese, timber, and hydrocarbons, but remain dependent on foreign capital, operators, and export infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Post-coup external balancing
frictionVectors.details: The transition government is diversifying partnerships beyond France, including toward China and Gulf states, while managing diplomatic pressure over its political timetable.

highlights: Senegal remains the decisive economic and security partner
Port access and fisheries shape sovereignty pressures

frictionVectors.title: Senegal-linked infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegalese trade corridors, energy links, and regional security cooperation, limiting room for independent infrastructure and resource policy.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and maritime control
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and limited enforcement capacity continue to threaten coastal livelihoods and raise concerns about licensing transparency and loss of marine resources.

highlights: Debt restructuring constrains strategic economic autonomy
Gold and emerging minerals remain central to resource sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector leakage and illegal mining
frictionVectors.details: Unregulated mining damages farmland and waterways while illicit networks and foreign-linked buyers capture value that the state struggles to tax and formalize.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Ghana is seeking more local processing and stronger control over lithium and other minerals, but fiscal pressure increases its dependence on external investors and lenders.

highlights: Bauxite wealth is expanding without equivalent domestic transformation
Simandou is reshaping regional infrastructure and foreign leverage

frictionVectors.title: Simandou and bauxite dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Singaporean, and other foreign-backed consortia dominate major mining and rail investments, creating jobs and infrastructure but leaving Guinea exposed to external control of export corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Military transition and resource governance
frictionVectors.details: The junta uses mining renegotiation to strengthen state leverage, while uncertainty over elections and contracts raises risks of politicized licensing and investor-driven concessions.

highlights: Cashew exports remain the backbone of a fragile economy
Political instability limits effective control of ports and borders

frictionVectors.title: Cashew value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country exports most cashews with limited processing, leaving farmers and state revenues vulnerable to foreign traders, price swings, and weak transport infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Port, narcotics, and regional influence
frictionVectors.details: Bissau's port and maritime routes remain vulnerable to political patronage and transnational trafficking, while Senegal and other regional actors retain substantial security influence.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is diversifying financing partners while renegotiating the fiscal burden of major infrastructure projects. Chinese lending, Western budget support, and Gulf investment remain important sources of leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Logistics Competition
frictionVectors.details: Nairobi is balancing Mombasa modernization, Lamu development, and regional transport links against competing interests from Gulf, Chinese, and neighboring-state investors.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water exports to South Africa provide crucial revenue but deepen structural dependence on Pretoria. Delays, cost escalation, and disputes over compensation constrain Lesotho's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Remittance and Industrial Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho remains highly exposed to South African labor markets and foreign-owned textile investment, limiting domestic control over employment and industrial policy.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Gold Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign mining companies remain central to exports and fiscal revenue, but concession terms, local employment, and environmental safeguards continue to raise sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Monrovia Port Influence
frictionVectors.details: Port modernization and logistics investment are essential to Liberia's growth, yet reliance on external operators and financiers creates strategic exposure over customs, trade, and maritime infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Oil Authorities
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks continue to contest control over oil facilities, budgets, and export routes. This fragments national sovereignty and leaves production vulnerable to coercive shutdowns.

frictionVectors.title: External Military Footprints
frictionVectors.details: Foreign states and private military actors retain influence through security partnerships, arms, and political sponsorship. Their presence complicates reunification and limits independent control of strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel and Cobalt Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large mining projects attract foreign capital and provide export earnings, but Madagascar retains limited bargaining power over technology, processing, and revenue distribution.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Transport Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Weak electricity and transport systems increase reliance on external financiers and contractors. This constrains the state's ability to secure domestic value from minerals, agriculture, and ports.

highlights: Mining expansion competes with fiscal survival

frictionVectors.title: Critical minerals and foreign capital
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is promoting uranium, rare earths and niobium projects to diversify beyond agriculture, but financing and ownership remain heavily dependent on foreign investors. Weak state capacity limits local value capture and oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and fertilizer dependence
frictionVectors.details: Persistent power shortages and reliance on imported fuel and fertilizer leave Malawi exposed to external price shocks. IMF-backed reforms improve macroeconomic discipline but reduce near-term room for sovereign investment.

highlights: Russian security ties deepen amid Western rupture

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector sovereignty disputes
frictionVectors.details: The military government is seeking a larger state share and tighter control over gold production, creating friction with foreign mining companies and raising concerns about contract stability. Informal and illicit flows remain difficult to regulate.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security and infrastructure isolation
frictionVectors.details: The withdrawal of French and international forces and the breakdown of regional cooperation have increased dependence on Russian-linked security support. Conflict and sanctions risks threaten transport corridors, power reliability and access to export markets.

highlights: Gas era begins under foreign-led development

frictionVectors.title: Greater Tortue Ahmeyim gas dependence
frictionVectors.details: The offshore gas project with Senegal, operated by BP and Kosmos Energy, offers major fiscal and energy benefits but leaves Mauritania reliant on foreign technology, capital and export infrastructure. Production delays and revenue-sharing arrangements remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Mining, ports and green-hydrogen positioning
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed iron-ore and renewable-energy projects could diversify the economy, but their scale risks reinforcing an enclave model with limited domestic processing. Control of ports, railways and land is becoming a central sovereignty concern.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos and Diego Garcia settlement
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius continues pressing its claim over the Chagos Archipelago while negotiating arrangements that preserve strategic use of Diego Garcia. The issue directly links territorial sovereignty, US-UK security interests and relations with India.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean infrastructure balancing
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius is balancing strong Indian ties with Chinese commercial engagement in ports, logistics and construction. External competition creates opportunities for investment but increases pressure to avoid strategic overdependence.

highlights: Renewables and phosphates reinforce strategic autonomy
Western Sahara remains the core sovereignty test

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara recognition contest
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is converting diplomatic recognition of its autonomy plan into economic and infrastructure commitments, while Algeria and the Polisario Front reject Moroccan sovereignty. Investment and trade through the territory remain politically contested.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign dependence in strategic industries
frictionVectors.details: Automotive, renewable-energy and port projects with European, Gulf and Chinese partners expand Morocco's industrial base but create exposure to external technology, markets and capital. Control of phosphate value chains and energy infrastructure remains a key sovereignty priority.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado security corridor
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent activity continues to shape access to offshore gas projects, leaving Mozambique reliant on foreign security support and multinational risk management.

frictionVectors.title: LNG contract asymmetry
frictionVectors.details: International operators and lenders retain substantial leverage over project terms, while local processing, jobs, and fiscal capture remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore oil bargaining
frictionVectors.details: New offshore discoveries could strengthen Namibia's fiscal position, but foreign-led exploration creates pressure for tougher local-content and revenue-sharing rules.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic infrastructure financing
frictionVectors.details: Port, rail, renewable-energy, and hydrogen projects attract competing external investors, requiring careful balancing of Chinese, European, Gulf, and regional interests.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and uranium realignment
frictionVectors.details: The junta is renegotiating relationships around uranium and oil while seeking alternative partners, but sanctions, border insecurity, and limited technical capacity constrain sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Alliance shift toward Russia and regional partners
frictionVectors.details: The withdrawal of Western forces and closer ties with Russia have reduced one form of external dependence while creating new security, financing, and infrastructure dependencies.

frictionVectors.title: Upstream capital dependence
frictionVectors.details: International oil companies remain central to deepwater investment and technology, while insecurity, theft, and regulatory uncertainty limit Nigeria's ability to capture full value.

frictionVectors.title: Power and pipeline bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable electricity and fragile gas infrastructure undermine domestic industrialization, increasing dependence on imported fuel, foreign contractors, and external financing.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo mineral scrutiny
frictionVectors.details: Allegations concerning cross-border support and mineral flows from eastern DRC continue to generate diplomatic pressure, complicating Rwanda's claims to a rules-based regional role.

frictionVectors.title: External finance concentration
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda retains strong administrative control over strategic projects, but dependence on donors, Gulf capital, and foreign technology limits full autonomy in infrastructure and resource development.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE LICENSING
frictionVectors.details: Unproven petroleum prospects attract foreign operators, but São Tomé and Príncipe lacks the capital and technical capacity to control exploration terms independently. Revenue expectations remain ahead of confirmed commercial production.

frictionVectors.title: GULF OF GUINEA SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: The country depends on regional and external partners for maritime surveillance and anti-piracy capabilities, limiting autonomous control over its offshore zone.

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON CONTRACTS
frictionVectors.details: New oil and gas production strengthens state revenues, but foreign operators and lenders retain major technical and financial influence. Dakar is seeking greater local participation without disrupting investment or production.

frictionVectors.title: FISHERIES PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Industrial and foreign fishing activity continues to generate disputes over access, transparency, and coastal livelihoods. Enforcement capacity is improving but remains uneven across Senegal's maritime zone.

frictionVectors.title: TUNA AND EEZ CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles benefits from a valuable maritime zone but must balance foreign fishing access against domestic value capture and conservation. Dependence on external fleets and monitoring support constrains full sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: INDIAN OCEAN STRATEGIC COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Port, surveillance, and maritime-security cooperation with India, France, China, and other partners creates leverage and investment opportunities. It also exposes the archipelago to pressure to align with competing regional security agendas.

frictionVectors.title: IRON ORE AND RUTILE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-linked mining companies and commodity markets continue to shape export earnings and fiscal stability. The government's push for better terms and domestic processing faces strong investor and infrastructure constraints.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND CORRIDOR CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Mining logistics depend on externally financed ports, roads, rail, and power infrastructure. These arrangements can improve capacity while concentrating strategic influence in foreign operators and creditors.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Federal authorities still rely heavily on foreign military, training, and financial support to secure territory and maritime approaches. Divergent interests among Türkiye, Gulf states, neighboring countries, and Western partners complicate unified national control.

frictionVectors.title: MARITIME AND ENERGY DEALS
frictionVectors.details: Offshore hydrocarbon exploration and port-related agreements offer potential sovereign revenue but are contested by federal member states and neighboring governments. Weak institutions and unresolved jurisdictional disputes limit Somalia's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is balancing Western, Chinese, and Gulf interest in platinum-group metals, manganese, and rare-earth supply chains. Regulatory uncertainty and infrastructure weaknesses limit Pretoria's ability to capture more downstream value.

frictionVectors.title: Logistics and electricity strain
frictionVectors.details: Chronic rail, port, and electricity constraints weaken sovereign control over mineral exports and increase dependence on private operators and foreign capital. Efforts to reform Transnet and Eskom remain politically contested.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan pipeline vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's oil exports remain dependent on infrastructure crossing war-torn Sudan, exposing revenue flows to conflict disruption and external bargaining. The arrangement sharply limits Juba's strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of oil finance
frictionVectors.details: International oil firms, trading intermediaries, and neighboring states retain substantial influence over production, transport, and payment channels. Weak institutions and renewed internal conflict reduce the government's ability to secure transparent national returns.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and wartime supply chains
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and export routes are entangled with armed networks and external buyers, particularly across the Gulf and regional corridors. This diverts resource wealth away from state institutions and funds continued conflict.

frictionVectors.title: Port and military competition
frictionVectors.details: Sudan's Red Sea coast has become a focus of competing foreign security, port, and basing interests. The war reduces Khartoum's bargaining power and increases the risk that infrastructure concessions are exchanged for military support.

frictionVectors.title: LNG project bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking stronger local-content, fiscal, and domestic-energy benefits from major offshore gas development while negotiating with international investors. Delays reflect Dar es Salaam's effort to preserve sovereignty without deterring capital.

frictionVectors.title: Ports and strategic corridors
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, rail, and trade-corridor projects are expanding Tanzania's regional leverage but create exposure to debt, concession, and geopolitical competition. Dar es Salaam is balancing Chinese, Gulf, Western, and neighboring-state interests.

frictionVectors.title: Port influence and concessions
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé remains central to Togo's trade and regional logistics strategy, with foreign operators and financiers shaping infrastructure capacity. This creates revenue opportunities but leaves strategic chokepoints vulnerable to external influence.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate resources provide fiscal value but limited downstream industrial capture, leaving Togo exposed to commodity cycles and external buyers. State efforts to modernize production compete with financing and technology dependence.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing leverage
frictionVectors.details: European funding and migration cooperation give the EU influence over Tunisian policymaking while fiscal stress limits Tunis's bargaining room.

frictionVectors.title: Gas and electricity exposure
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains dependent on Algerian gas and imported energy, constraining sovereign control over power costs and industrial competitiveness.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and sanctions pressure
frictionVectors.details: The oil pipeline with Tanzania is central to Uganda's resource strategy but faces sustained environmental, legal, and financing pressure from Western actors.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed transport and energy projects expand infrastructure capacity while increasing exposure to external contractors, debt obligations, and commodity-linked bargaining.

highlights: Copper diplomacy is becoming more assertive

frictionVectors.title: Copper ownership and value capture
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is pressing investors to expand local processing and fiscal contributions, but foreign control of major copper assets still limits domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and creditor conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and multilateral support stabilize public finances but constrain policy autonomy and expose strategic infrastructure decisions to creditor scrutiny.

highlights: Critical minerals draw aggressive foreign competition

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and platinum external control
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, South African, and other foreign investors dominate capital-intensive mining, while Zimbabwe struggles to enforce beneficiation and transparent revenue-sharing requirements.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and currency leakage
frictionVectors.details: Informal gold channels, sanctions-related payment constraints, and persistent currency instability reduce the state's ability to retain full value from mineral exports.
